extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, natural-rights theory, and legal/political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of principles governing parental authority, the status of children, the ends and limits of marriage, and the origins/distinction of political (civil) society. Explains when parental power exists, what it may legitimately do, and how it differs from political sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power is shared by both parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental authority (parental power) belongs to mother as well as father; it is not peculiarly the father's right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues against calling the power 'absolute dominion' or treating it as solely paternal — the law of God and positive law join mother and father together (e.g., 'Honour thy father and thy mother'). Examples: cases where mother provides sole care (widow, separated societies) show mother has the same practical authority; hypothetical customs (one woman with multiple husbands) undermine a bare begetting-based paternal claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental authority is temporary and tied to minority
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents have rule/jurisdiction over children only during the child's imperfect state of infancy/minority; this subjection is temporary and falls away as age and reason grow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses metaphor of swaddling clothes; parental bonds loosen with age and reason until they 'drop quite off.' The governing power terminates with nonage; education/tutorship may be delegated and is alienable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental duty: preserve, nourish, and educate offspring
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents are by the law of nature under obligation to preserve, nourish, and educate their children until they can provide for themselves and govern their actions by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty is grounded in natural obligation and accountability to the Maker; it is the basis of the parents' temporary rule and justifies restraint for children's good rather than ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children are born equal in jurisdiction but may have precedence
rubrics_metrics.description: All men are equal in respect of jurisdiction or dominion one over another; however, distinctions (age, virtue, merit, birth, alliance) may give precedence without violating natural equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies different senses of equality — political/jurisdictional equality vs. other social precedences. The equality relevant here is the equal right to natural freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law applies to agents only when promulgated to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: A person is under a law only when that law is promulgated to him through reason; infants, not having use of reason, are not immediately under the law of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since law directs a free and intelligent agent, someone incapable of understanding cannot properly be bound by that law; hence parental governance stands in loco of the child's own reason until the child attains it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of law is to preserve and enlarge freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Law is not primarily limitation but the direction of a free agent for general good; where there is no law there is no freedom — true liberty is regulated freedom, not licence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects notion that liberty is doing what one likes; freedom is to order one's life within the bounds of law so as not to be subject to arbitrary will of another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents act for the child's will while child lacks reason
rubrics_metrics.description: While the child lacks understanding to direct his will, someone else (parents/guardian) must will and prescribe for him; the parent 'must prescribe to his will, and regulate his actions' until the child attains reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames parental rule as necessary stewardship, not usurpation of child's freedom; once the child attains a state that made the father free, the son is equally free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom is attained at an age/state of reason (variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A person's freedom and capacity to dispose of property and actions depends on attainment of reason/maturity; legal ages (e.g., 21 in England) are conventions that presume such capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The precise point is easier for sense than for learned determination; commonwealths sometimes mark the age when public acts (oaths, fealty) begin to be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorrigible incapacity justifies perpetual guardianship
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons who never attain sufficient reason (lunatics, idiots, certain innocents) remain under guardianship and are never set free to dispose of their own will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Hooker and others: such cases are continued under tutelage for their protection; guardians employ reason of others to seek their good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental power limited to discipline necessary for child's welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: Parental authority extends only to such discipline as is necessary and effectual to give strength, health, and rectitude to body and mind, and to fit children to be useful to themselves and others; it does not include legislative power over life, liberty, or estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly denies fathers' claim to absolute arbitrary dominion, capital punishments, or perpetual laws binding children beyond minority; parental command intended for education and necessary labour when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor/respect owed to parents is perpetual and distinct from obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Children owe perpetual honour, reverence, support, and compliance to parents as gratitude for benefits received, but this does not equate to perpetual obedience or parental legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honour ties the child from injuring or endangering parents and obliges defence/assistance throughout life; yet honour does not give parents dominion over property or prescribe all actions of adult children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental powers (education) are alienable and delegable
rubrics_metrics.description: A father may transfer the tuition/education of his son (e.g., by apprenticeship), thereby discharging parts of his authority during that time; foster-parents or tutors can hold the practical power of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows parental power is linked to care and can pass to others who perform the nutritive/educative functions; mere begetting without care confers little authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental promise of inheritance ties obedience by reward, not natural duty
rubrics_metrics.description: A father's ability to bestow estates creates a tie on children's obedience (through expectation of inheritance), but this is not a natural paternal right to political allegiance — it is a voluntary acceptance of conditions attached to the inheritance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a Frenchman promising land to an Englishman can secure obedience by hope of estate; children remain free to choose society but if they accept ancestral inheritance they accept its conditions (including political subjection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power is distinct from paternal power and arises by consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Political sovereignty is not the same as paternal authority; public government and monarchy arose from tacit or explicit consent of families/children, not from a natural right of fathers to rule as monarchs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues historical route from household rule to kingship was by consent and adaptation of executive power, and refutes the Filmer-style claim that princes trace authority by paternal right; uses example of strangers punished in a household by the head acting as executive of natural law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal society is a voluntary compact with limited ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage/ conjugal society is a voluntary compact chiefly for procreation, mutual support, and the care of offspring; it need not confer absolute power on the husband and its duration is tied to the needs of the young.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares human conjugal duration to animals, argues human pair-bond lasts longer because offspring need extended support. Husband may have primacy in common interests as 'abler and stronger' but wife retains separate property rights and may separate where contract/natural right allow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil magistrate adjudicates but does not supply conjugal essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: In civil society, magistrates do not abridge natural rights necessary to marriage's ends (procreation, support), but only decide controversies between spouses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because absolute husband sovereignty is unnecessary for conjugal ends, societies that disallow such power still permit matrimony; the state's role is regulatory and adjudicatory rather than constitutive of conjugal power.
